Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

No remembering now when the apple sapling was blown almost out of the ground. No telling how, with all the other trees around, it alone was struck. It must have been luck, he thought for years, so close to the house it grew. It must have been night. Change is a thing one sleeps through when young, and he was young. If there was a weakness in the earth, a give he went down on his knees to find and feel the limits of, there is no longer. If there was one random blow from above the way he's come to know from years in this place, the roots were stronger. Whatever the case, he has watched this tree survive wind ripping at his roof for nights on end, heats and blights that left little else alive. No remembering now... A day's changes mean all to him and all days come down to one clear pane through which he sees among all the other trees this leaning, clenched, unyielding one that seems cast in the form of a blast that would have killed it, as if something at the heart of things, and with the heart of things, had willed it.

Keywords: Change, Whatever

No one remembers now the day the apple sapling was nearly torn from the ground. Nor can anyone explain how, among all the other trees that stood around it, this one alone was struck. For years he thought it must have been mere chance—it grew so close to the house. It must have happened in the night. Change is something one sleeps through when young, and young he was. I no longer remember the exact circumstances of how the apple sapling came to be nearly uprooted and struck, while all the trees surrounding it were left untouched. The specific details have faded from memory, lost to the passage of time. What remains is only the outcome: that against all reasonable expectation, that single young tree suffered where its neighbors were spared.

If I am honest, I can attribute its survival to nothing more than luck. It occurs to me now how often change happens without our notice—how the most decisive moments slip past us unmarked, particularly during those unaware years of youth when we are too consumed by living to observe our own lives. Something turned in the fate of that tree, and I was not paying attention.

I have looked, in the years since, for some explanation. I have searched for a weakness in the earth around it, some flaw in the soil that might account for what happened, or for evidence of a random blow delivered from above. But I have found nothing. Whatever it was that threatened the sapling, the tree's roots simply proved the stronger. It held to the ground more firmly than the force that sought to tear it free.

And it has gone on holding. The tree has endured relentless winds that bent it season after season, extreme heat that scorched the land, and blights that killed nearly everything else that grew around it. Where other trees withered and fell, it remained. Its resilience has been nothing short of remarkable—a quiet, stubborn insistence on continuing.

Now, looking out through my window, I see it still: leaning, clenched, its trunk twisted as though it had been shaped by the very force that should have destroyed it. There is something in its posture that suggests it was not merely spared but formed by its near-destruction, molded by the blow it survived. And I cannot help but feel, when I regard it, that something at the very heart of existence willed it to live.
outputs.L4:
# The Apple Tree

When I was young, a storm came through our valley with a fury I have never since forgotten. It tore across the hills in the black hours before dawn, and by morning the orchard lay ruined—trunks split, branches scattered like broken bones across the sodden grass. I remember walking out with my father, both of us silent, surveying what the night had taken.

Every tree had fallen. Every tree but one.

There it stood, the old apple at the orchard's edge, and though I have lived a long life since, I have never stopped returning to it in my mind. I can see it still: leaning hard against the wind that was no longer there, its roots half-lifted from the earth, clinging to the soil by some stubbornness I could not name. The storm had seized it, wrenched it, nearly torn it free—and yet it held. Where its brothers had surrendered and lay dead, this one alone refused.

I have spent years wondering why. What was it in this tree, and not the others, that would not let go? I have studied the shape it kept ever after—for it never straightened again. It grew crooked and bent, curved permanently against the memory of that wind, as though the storm had pressed itself forever into the grain of the wood. The very force that should have killed it had instead become its form.

And this is what I have come to believe: that shape was not defeat but defiance. The tree did not merely endure the storm; it took the storm into itself and made of it a posture, a stance, a way of standing in the world. To look at that bent and knotted trunk was to see resistance made visible—survival written into the body of a living thing.

I think now that this is no small matter. In that crooked tree I glimpse something at the very heart of existence: a will that runs deeper than circumstance, older than reason, insistent beyond all sense. The world moves toward ruin, toward scattering and rest, and yet something in life leans back against it, holds fast, refuses the easy surrender of the fallen.

The apple tree taught me this, though it spoke no word. It survived, and in surviving it revealed a truth I have carried all my days—that to be shaped by what would destroy us, and to stand anyway, is perhaps the deepest meaning we are given.
outputs.L5:
# Change: The Only Constant

Change is one of those inevitable forces that shapes every aspect of our lives, whether we welcome it or not. From the shifting seasons to the evolution of technology, from personal growth to global transformations, change is constant and unstoppable.

## Embracing the Inevitable

There's a certain freedom in accepting that change will happen regardless of our resistance. When we adopt a "whatever comes, comes" attitude, we release ourselves from the anxiety of trying to control every outcome. This doesn't mean being passive or indifferent—rather, it means developing the flexibility to adapt and grow.

## The Power of "Whatever"

The word "whatever" often gets a bad reputation. People associate it with apathy or dismissiveness. But there's wisdom in this simple word. Sometimes saying "whatever" is a healthy way of letting go of things beyond our control. It's a reminder that not every battle is worth fighting and not every situation requires our emotional investment.

## Finding Balance

The key lies in knowing when to embrace change and when to let things be. Some changes we can influence and direct; others we simply have to accept. The challenge is developing the wisdom to tell the difference.

Life will keep changing whether we're ready or not. So perhaps the healthiest approach is to prepare for what we can, accept what we cannot, and greet each new day with an open mind and a resilient spirit.

Whatever happens next, we have the power to choose how we respond.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about a leaning apple tree that survived being nearly blown out of the ground when it was young, using rhyme and reflecting on how an old man sees it now.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Leaning Apple Tree

Half-toppled in a springtime gale,
when roots were young and thin and pale,
it should have died there in the mud—
uprooted by that howling flood.

But something held. A single thread
of stubborn root refused the dead,
and so it grew, though bent and low,
at angles no straight tree would know.

An old man watches from his chair,
his own spine curved beyond repair,
and sees within that leaning limb
a kindred thing that speaks to him.

For he too weathered wind and rain,
was nearly lost, then rose again,
and though he stoops toward the sod,
he still puts forth his fruit, by God.

The blossoms come each faithful May,
the apples fall and roll away,
and children climb its crooked spine
to taste the sweetness of the vine.

The old man smiles. He understands
that beauty lives in broken hands,
that what survives the fiercest blast
grows richer, sweeter, deeper, last.

So let them stand upon the hill—
the bent old man, the tree that will
outlive him yet, and lean, and give,
and teach the young how best to live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective, rhyming poem in which a man contemplates a weathered tree outside his house and wonders whether its survival was luck or some deeper will at the heart of things.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Weathered Tree**

Beyond my window, gnarled and grey,
it leans against the fading day,
a tree that storms have tried to break,
that lightning split for splitting's sake.

I've watched it stand through forty years
of drought that dried the farmers' tears,
through winters wild with cracking ice,
through summers scorched and paid in price.

Its bark is scarred, its limbs are bent,
half of its noble crown is spent,
and yet each spring, against the odds,
it lifts green hands as if to gods.

I wonder, in the quiet gloom,
what spared it from an early tomb—
was it mere chance, a random grace,
that let it hold this stubborn place?

Or does some deeper current run
beneath the roots, beneath the sun,
a patient will that shapes and saves,
that carries oaks across their graves?

I cannot say. The wind replies
in whispers that I can't surmise.
Perhaps the luck and will are one,
the same slow work of rain and sun.

And so I watch it, old and torn,
still standing where the storms were born,
and think that whether fate or fate's
own accident, it simply waits—

as I do now, grown grey and slow,
uncertain what I ought to know,
but sure of this, if nothing more:
we both are here. We both endure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical poem exploring themes of endurance, memory, and change, centered on a single tree that withstood storms, blights, and heat over many years.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Standing Witness

Here where the meadow meets the failing light,
I have kept my station through a hundred years,
rooted in the argument of soil and stone,
learning the long grammar of endurance.

*

I remember the first storm—
how the sky turned the color of a bruise
and the wind came looking for something to break.
I bent. I did not know then that bending
was its own kind of strength,
that the trees who would not yield
lay by morning like fallen soldiers,
their roots upturned and grasping at nothing.

*

The blight came quiet as a rumor,
a whisper in my leaves, a yellowing,
a slow subtraction of my summer green.
I dropped my sickness like a coat
and stood there naked, waiting,
counting the days in the only way I know—
by patience, by the turning,
by the faith that light returns.

*

And the heat—oh, the years the rains forgot us,
when the ground cracked open like old lips
and thirst became my only language.
I sent my roots down deeper into memory,
down to where the water hides its secrets,
and I drank the dark, and I survived.

*

Children who once climbed my lower branches
walk slower now beneath my shade,
their hair gone silver as the underside of leaves.
I have outlived their laughter and their grief,
outlived the swing that hung from my east arm,
the initials carved into my patient bark—
love that swore forever
and meant it for a little while.

*

Everything that touched me left its mark.
Every storm is written in my rings,
each drought a narrow year,
each season of abundance
a widening, a generosity of growth.
I am my own long history,
a book that only fire could ever read aloud.

*

Change is the only weather that stays.
The field around me shifts its borders,
the fences rust, the farmhouse leans and falls,
and still I stand—not stubborn,
but agreeable to time,
willing to be shaped by what would break me,
willing to hold my ground and let go both at once.

*

So let the next wind come.
Let the seasons do their patient work.
I have learned the oldest secret of the standing:
that to endure is not to stay unchanged,
but to carry every wound as ring and record,
to be made larger by the very things
that tried to bring me down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that begins and repeats the phrase "No remembering now" and tells the story of a tree that grew despite an early trauma, ending with the idea that something willed it to survive.
counterfactuals.output:
**No Remembering Now**

No remembering now
the axe that missed its mark,
the split bark weeping sap
into the frozen dark.

No remembering now
the sapling bent and bowed,
the winter that came early,
the branches snapped and plowed

beneath the weight of ice,
the deer that stripped the skin,
the season when the roots
first felt the rot begin.

No remembering now—
and yet the trunk grew wide,
the scar became a hollow
where the owls would nest and hide.

No remembering now
the thousand ways it bent
around the wound, the knot,
the crooked argument

it made against the sky,
each ring a buried year,
each spring a stubborn answer
to the frost it could not fear.

No remembering now
how close it came to none,
how thin the thread that held it
turning green toward the sun.

But something in the dark,
some green and wordless vow,
some will beneath the willing—
*live*, it said. *Grow now.*

And so it did. And does.
No remembering how.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemplative free-verse-style poem with internal rhymes about aging, place, and a lone apple tree that seems shaped by the very force that should have destroyed it.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Apple Tree at the Field's Edge**

There's a wind that has learned this hill by heart,
that has practiced its part for a hundred slow years,
and the tree—that old tree—leans east
where it was pressed, where the gusts confessed
their long intention to break what would not bend.

But breaking became a bending instead.
The wood read the weather and grew toward its threat,
each knuckle and knot a record, a plot
of storms it forgot to die from.

I am older now than I meant to be.
The county has changed; the road they arranged
runs closer, louder, a river of steel.
Still I come to feel the same rough bark,
the same dark furrow where lightning once burrowed
and left, instead of an ending, a scar
that widened to gnarl, to a strange kind of star
the branches all circle around.

Consider the shape that survival can take:
not straight, not spared, but stubbornly paired
with the very thing that came to unmake it.
The apple tree wears its wounding like weather,
holds season to season together with roots
that grip what would rip it away.

And I think, as the gray light lengthens the day,
that a place is a pressure, a slow-turning grief,
that a life is the leaf we manage to keep
where the wind meant to strip us bare—

that we, too, are bent to a beautiful there,
shaped by the force that we swore
would be more than we were.

Yet here is the fruit. Small, sour, and true.
The tree does not know that it fought its way through.
It only keeps offering, autumn on autumn,
what the storm, in the end, could not hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
